summary:
We developed AEGIS, an interactive web platform and scientific engine that systematically discovers, characterizes, and ranks Earth-based planetary analogs for permanent Moon (Artemis) and Mars landing sites. The platform features an Autonomous Discovery Engine with an on-the-fly GPS coordinate probe, interactive Leaflet mapping, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) microwave penetration modeling, and space hardware testing simulators.
To meet the challenge of identifying Moon and Mars analogs—and looking beyond overstudied benchmarks—AEGIS uncovers novel, understudied terrestrial sites (e.g., the Batagaika permafrost megaslump for Martian sheet ice, Harrat Ash Shaam lava tubes for lunar underground shelters, and Lonar basalt impact crater). Sites are objectively scored via the Planetary Analog Similarity Index (PASI) across six dimensions (topography, thermal swings, mineralogy, cryosphere, radar dielectrics, and hardware testability), while explicitly accounting for where analogies break down due to gravity, atmospheric, and radiation discrepancies.
Testing rovers, cryogenic drills, and EVA suits in realistic terrestrial environments is vital to preventing catastrophic mission failures. AEGIS provides space agencies and engineers with a data-driven tool to pair specific mission risks with targeted terrestrial proving grounds before launch.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

AEGIS is an interactive geospatial intelligence platform and scientific engine designed to discover, evaluate, and benchmark Earth environments that mirror surface conditions at high-priority Moon (Artemis Base Camp, Shackleton Crater, Marius Hills) and Mars (Jezero Crater, Arcadia Planitia, Mawrth Vallis) landing sites.

The system works through several core features:

  • Autonomous Planetary Analog Discovery Engine (APADE): Scans global Earth observation grids to identify unconventional analog candidates. It includes an On-the-Fly GPS Coordinate Diagnostic Probe, allowing users to click anywhere on Earth or input custom coordinates to dynamically calculate analog fidelity, microwave radar skin depth, and physical breakdown points.
    1. Topography & Roughness (StopoS_{\text{topo}}Stopo​): Slope gradients, crater morphology, and RMS surface roughness.
    2. Thermal Extremes (SthermS_{\text{therm}}Stherm​): Diurnal temperature variations, cryogenic minimums, and thermal inertia.
    3. Geology & Geochemistry (SgeoS_{\text{geo}}Sgeo​): Basaltic composition, impact shock metamorphism, and phyllosilicate clays.
    4. Cryosphere & Permafrost (ScryoS_{\text{cryo}}Scryo​): Ground ice stability and sub-zero permafrost depth.
    5. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SsarS_{\text{sar}}Ssar​): C-band radar backscatter, dielectric permittivity (εr\varepsilon_rεr​), and loss tangents (tan⁡δ\tan\deltatanδ).
    6. Operations & Testing Utility (SopsS_{\text{ops}}Sops​): Hardware deployment feasibility and terrain traversability.
  • SAR Penetration Sounding Lab: Computes microwave skin depths (δp\delta_pδp​) in dry media and ice, comparing CSA RADARSAT-1 and ESA Sentinel-1 data against planetary sounders (LRO Mini-RF and MRO SHARAD).
  • Mission Testing Simulator: Matches specific engineering risks (rover wheel slip, cryogenic ice coring, space suit abrasion) to targeted field sites and validation protocols.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Moves Beyond Overstudied Sites: Avoids sole reliance on traditional sites like Devon Island and the Atacama Desert, which fail to capture specific planetary regimes such as intact lunar lava tube skylights or active permafrost retrogressive thaw slumps.
  • Multi-Dimensional Quantification: Replaces qualitative "looks like Mars" guesswork with an empirical, weighted 0–100% similarity score across six physical domains.
  • Scientific Honesty & Rigor: Features a dedicated "Where the Analogy Breaks Down" module detailing differences in gravity, atmospheric pressure, and radiation so engineers do not misinterpret terrestrial field data.
  • Open & Exportable: Generates standardized JSON data packages for mission architects, research institutions, and field expeditions.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Field testing on Earth is essential to derisking multi-billion-dollar space missions before launch. AEGIS directly impacts:

  • Mission De-risking: Prevents fatal hardware failures—such as rover entrapment on steep basalt talus or drill jamming in cryo-regolith—by directing teams to the highest-fidelity terrestrial testing grounds.
  • Resource Optimization: Enables space agencies (NASA, CSA, ESA) and commercial space partners to select cost-effective, logistically feasible testing sites tailored to specific subsystem requirements.
  • Planetary Science & Education: Serves as an open-access educational and research tool connecting planetary science with terrestrial Earth observation data.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python 3, HTML5, CSS3
  • Frontend Framework & Build System: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide React Icons
  • Geospatial & Visualization: Leaflet, React-Leaflet, Custom SVG Radar & Polarimetric Charts
    • NASA Earthdata & PDS: SRTM 30m DEM, ASTER GDEM v3, MODIS Land Surface Temperature (MOD11A1), Landsat-8/9, LRO Diviner Lunar Radiometer, LRO LOLA Topography, LROC NAC, MRO CRISM/SHARAD
    • Canadian Space Agency (CSA): RADARSAT-1 C-Band Open Data
    • European Space Agency (ESA): Copernicus Sentinel-1 (C-SAR) and Sentinel-2
  • Deployment & Version Control: Vercel (Edge deployment), Git, GitHub

5. How is your project creative?

  • Autonomous Discovery vs. Static Encyclopedias: Rather than just displaying a curated list, AEGIS introduces an autonomous scanner that searches global Earth observation rasters and lets users test any location on Earth via arbitrary GPS coordinates.
    • Batagaika Megaslump (Siberia): Massive permafrost retrogressive thaw slump exposing 650,000-year-old Yedoma ice wedges, simulating Martian scalloped depressions in Arcadia Planitia.
    • Harrat Ash Shaam (Jordan/Saudi Arabia): 40,000 km² basalt volcanic field with intact collapse skylights directly mirroring the Marius Hills lunar pit.
    • Dallol Hydrothermal Field (Ethiopia): Boiling, hyper-acidic brine pools (pH < 0) mirroring early Noachian lacustrine hydrothermal systems on Mars.
    • Lonar Crater (India): The only hypervelocity impact crater in continental flood basalt on Earth.
  • Physics-Based Multi-Agency Synthesis: Combines optical, thermal, radar altimetry, and microwave dielectric properties from three space agencies (NASA, CSA, ESA) into one unified diagnostic dashboard.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Physical & Environmental Limitations: Terrestrial analogs have clear constraints. We explicitly factored in:
    • Gravity: 1.0g on Earth vs. 0.166g on the Moon and 0.38g on Mars alters rover wheel sinkage, traction, and slope stability.
    • Atmosphere: Earth’s 1013 hPa atmosphere introduces convective cooling and moisture weathering, unlike the lunar vacuum (10−1210^{-12}10−12 hPa) or thin Martian air (~6 hPa).
    • Radiation: Earth’s magnetosphere blocks cosmic rays and solar particle events that extraterrestrial hardware must endure.
    • Biology & Water: Terrestrial biomes and meteoric precipitation contrast with sterile planetary surfaces.
  • Hardware Testing Realities: Evaluated operational constraints such as logistical accessibility, local regulations, environmental sensitivity, and hardware wear rates.
